messages.author: 3ab4461ff960be07
messages.subject: panel data models using R-INLA
parts:
Hello INLA people!

            Could you guys please suggest a website or any other freely available source where I can find examples on panel data models using the R-INLA package? By “panel data models”, I mean the ones:

             - where both X and Y variables are metric;

            - with some number of categories / groups / individuals, each of whom provide more than 1 pair of X and Y combinations;

            - where a researcher is interested in the effect of X on Y for each category / group / individual, as well as the overall effect of X on Y.

            I have gone through the Virgilio Gómez-Rubio’s book “Bayesian Inference with INLA”, but unfortunately could not find any suitable example in it.

            Thank you all guys for your time and considerations in regard to this matter!

           

            Sincerely,

            Rustam

messages.author: 334c7505e0b5cf65
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] panel data models using R-INLA
parts:
Hi,

It looks like you are looking for multilevel and/or longitudinal models. You may look at the example on the reaction time, in which the effect of time is different for each subject in the study:

https://becarioprecario.bitbucket.io/inla-gitbook/ch-multilevel.html#multilevel-models-for-longitudinal-data

Best,

Virgilio

parts:
Hi Virgilio,

 

It is so cool that you have answered! That example with the sleepstudy dataset is the one that I studied the most, but even though, frankly, I did not fully understand it, I am happy to hear that at least I have been on the right track.

Could you please clarify for me some points regarding that example? In particular, do the Figures 6 and 7 represent the overall effect of the main predictor on the response variable, as well as for each individual, respectively? Or do these Figures represent something a little bit different than what I am looking for? I am a little bit confused on that, because the description of the Figure 6 says “this model assumes the same slope of the effect of Days on the students”, but all 16 graphs of the Figure 6 show different slopes.

 

            Sincerely,

            Rustam

parts: Could you please clarify for me some points regarding that example? In particular, do the Figures 6 and 7 represent the overall effect of the main predictor on the response variable, as well as for each individual, respectively?

Figure 4.6 is placed right after the model with fixed effect and subject iid effects, which is unfortunate, because Figure 4.6 shows the estimates from a different model. Figure 4.7 shows a summary of the model fit that includes random slopes. Here, in order to represent the line, the posterior mean of the intercept and subject-slop are used.

Or do these Figures represent something a little bit different than what I am looking for? I am a little bit confused on that, because the description of the Figure 6 says “this model assumes the same slope of the effect of Days on the students”, but all 16 graphs of the Figure 6 show different slopes.

Yes. AS I said, the placement of the figure is unfortunate. I may change this in the book so that this Firme is shown a bit earlier in the text. In the printed version I guess this is not an issue. Also, please check the R code of the  book. Therein you will see how each figure is produced and you will get a better understanding of what is being plotted.

Best,

Virgilio
